claims.text: Machine-learning-guided mapping of the NM-HEA formation free-energy landscape will enable controlled nucleation and growth.
Controlled nucleation and growth will produce three-dimensional interconnected nanoframeworks with precise atomic mixing.
Conventional synthesis methods produce random noble-metal HEA nanoparticle ensembles with uncontrolled atomic distributions.
Real-time adjustment of temperature ramp, precursor concentration, and reducing environment can steer free-energy pathways during alloy formation.
NM-HEA synthesis involves nucleation and particle-coalescence processes.
High-temperature environments are relevant to HEA nanoparticle applications.
The synthesis uses multimetal precursor mixtures with near-equiatomic ratios.
The resulting structural mediator is a three-dimensional framework of interconnected HEA nanoparticles.
The nanoframework will have uniform atomic-level mixing and a controlled surface structure.
Machine-learning models can represent alloy thermodynamic phase-space or free-energy behavior.
Correlating synthesis parameters with free-energy profiles enables precise modulation of nucleation and growth dynamics.
Machine-learning control of nucleation and growth minimizes phase segregation.
Favoring energetically optimal formation pathways drives the development of an interconnected three-dimensional structure.
ML-guided synthesis will yield NM-HEA nanoframeworks with greater connectivity and atomic-scale uniformity than conventional synthesis.
Greater connectivity and atomic-scale uniformity will improve catalytic performance.
Mechanical alloying and arc melting produce less-controlled random nanoparticle assemblages and non-optimized three-dimensional structures.
Controlled nanoframework formation is limited to a parameter range in which the machine-learning model remains accurate.
Conditions outside the model's training domain may cause deviations from the desired architecture.
Elemental segregation and dynamic atomic motion complicate atomic-scale structural control in NM-HEA nanoparticles.
In situ aberration-corrected STEM can monitor atomic-scale structural and chemical evolution during heating of NM-HEA nanoparticles.
